Input vectors and positional encoding (absolute, relative, RoPE)
Add & Norm: residual connection and LayerNorm
Distinct roles of attention and FFN, and the block stack
Model families: BERT, GPT, T5 and MLM

sorular.konu: Why Transformers: attention instead of recurrence
sorular.soru: An RNN reads a sentence one token at a time. Why does this make training on very large data slow?
secenekler: Each token gets its own set of weights, so the model grows too large to train
Each token is compared with every other token, so the work grows very fast
Each step waits for the one before it, so the steps cannot run in parallel
Each token must first get a position signal, which adds many extra steps
sorular.aciklama: An RNN needs the result of one step before it can start the next, so its work forms a long chain. Comparing every token with every other token is what attention does, and that work runs in parallel.

sorular.konu: Why Transformers: attention instead of recurrence
sorular.soru: In a long story, a word near the end depends on a name from the first line. Why can attention handle this link more easily than an RNN?
secenekler: Attention links the two words directly, not through a long chain of steps
Attention keeps the name in its position vector, which all later words can read
Attention carries the name along the residual path from one word to the next
Attention lets the FFN at the last word read every earlier word in the story
sorular.aciklama: Attention gives the late word a direct path to the name, while an RNN must pass the name through every word in between. The residual path carries a vector from one layer to the next, not from one word to another.

sorular.konu: Input vectors and positional encoding (absolute, relative, RoPE)
sorular.soru: A model has full self-attention but no position signal. You change the order of the words in a sentence. What happens to each word's output vector?
secenekler: It changes, because each word now has different words next to it
It changes, because the dot products now see a new word order
It becomes the old output of the word that was in its place
It stays the same, and only the order of the outputs changes
sorular.aciklama: Without a position signal, attention sees the words only as a set, so each word gets the same weights and the same mix as before. New neighbors change nothing, because the model cannot tell which words are next to each other.

sorular.konu: Input vectors and positional encoding (absolute, relative, RoPE)
sorular.soru: With pure absolute positions, each token gets a signal for its own slot only. What must the model then work out by itself?
secenekler: The order of the words, since slot signals do not show any order
How far apart two tokens are, from their two slot signals
What each word means, since the slot signal replaces the word
Which tokens come later, so that it can hide them in training
sorular.aciklama: An absolute signal only says which slot a token is in, so the model must learn the gap between two tokens from both signals. The slots do show the order, so the missing part is the distance, which relative methods give directly.

sorular.soru: For the word 'it', attention puts weights on 'animal', 'street' and 'tired'. What is the updated vector of 'it' made of?
secenekler: The value vector of 'animal' alone, because it has the highest weight
A mix of their key vectors, with more from the words with high weights
The query vector of 'it', moved a little toward the word with the most weight
A mix of their value vectors, with more from the words with high weights
sorular.aciklama: The output is a weighted sum of value vectors, so every word adds some content and high-weight words add more. Keys are used only to find the weights, and the content itself comes from the values.

sorular.soru: Attention can be compared to looking for a book in a library. Which match of query, key and value fits best?
secenekler: Query: your question. Key: the label on each book. Value: the text inside
Query: the label on each book. Key: your question. Value: the text inside
Query: your question. Key: the text inside. Value: the label on each book
Query: the text inside. Key: the label on each book. Value: your question
sorular.aciklama: The query says what a token is looking for, the keys are checked against it, and the values hold the content that is taken. Swapping query and key mixes up who asks with what is checked.

sorular.soru: A word may need a link to its neighbor for grammar and a link to a far word for meaning. Which design helps the model learn both kinds of link at once?
secenekler: One head with a sharper softmax that picks the single best word
One head with a larger FFN that mixes both links inside each token
Several heads, so each head can learn its own pattern of links
Several position signals, one for near words and one for far words
sorular.aciklama: Each head has its own query, key and value weights, so one head can follow grammar while another follows meaning. A single head gives only one pattern of weights, and a sharper softmax only makes that pattern narrower.

sorular.konu: Add & Norm: residual connection and LayerNorm
sorular.soru: Early in training, a sublayer gives an update that is almost zero. With the residual path, what comes out of the Add step?
secenekler: A vector close to zero, so the old information fades away
Almost the old vector, so the information it carried is kept
A mix of the other token vectors, chosen by attention weights
The first token embedding again, so the block starts fresh
sorular.aciklama: The residual path adds the old vector to the update, so a tiny update leaves the vector almost as it was. A vector near zero is what you would get without the residual path, because only the update would pass on.

sorular.konu: Add & Norm: residual connection and LayerNorm
sorular.soru: After each residual sum, the Transformer applies LayerNorm. What is the main job of this step?
secenekler: It keeps the numbers in each token vector in a stable range
It makes the attention weights of each token add up to one
It hides the future tokens from each position in the text
It mixes information between the tokens of the same sentence
sorular.aciklama: LayerNorm shifts and scales the numbers of each token vector, so they stay in a safe range from block to block. Making weights add up to one is the job of softmax inside attention.

sorular.konu: Distinct roles of attention and FFN, and the block stack
sorular.soru: Suppose you remove every attention layer and keep only the FFNs. Which ability does the model lose?
secenekler: Applying a non-linear change to each token vector on its own
Keeping each token's old vector through the residual path
Letting a token use other tokens to update its own vector
Giving each token a signal that shows its place in the text
sorular.aciklama: Attention is the only step where tokens share information, so without it each token is processed alone. The FFN still makes its non-linear change, but it works on one position at a time.

sorular.konu: Distinct roles of attention and FFN, and the block stack
sorular.soru: A Transformer repeats the same kind of block many times. What does the model gain from this stacking?
secenekler: Each block reads a new part of the text, so long inputs fit
Each block makes the sequence shorter, until one vector is left
Each block holds one head, so stacking gives the model more views
Each block adds more context, so token vectors grow richer
sorular.aciklama: In every block the tokens share information again and then improve it, so the vectors carry more and more context. The sequence length stays the same through the whole stack, so no block makes it shorter.

sorular.soru: Model A labels each word of a finished sentence. Model B writes a reply one token at a time. Why can only model A use full attention?
secenekler: Model A has the whole text, but model B must not see later tokens
Model A has short texts, so looking both ways costs very little
Model B needs its position signal, and full attention would erase it
Model A learns by next-token prediction, which needs both directions
sorular.aciklama: Full attention is fine when the whole input is given and no next token must be guessed. The rule is about cheating, not cost, because model B could copy the next token if it saw later ones.

sorular.soru: In training, a decoder handles all positions of a sentence at once. But when it writes new text, it makes one token per step. Why?
secenekler: The causal mask is turned off when writing, so the work must slow down
Later tokens depend on earlier ones, and those must be chosen first
The encoder must run again from the start before each new token
The FFN works on one position at a time, so the tokens must take turns
sorular.aciklama: In training the whole target text is already known, so all positions can run at once under a causal mask. When writing, each next token is known only after the one before it is chosen, and the mask stays on in both cases.

sorular.soru: A translation model has an encoder for the source text and a decoder for the target text. Which problem does cross-attention solve?
secenekler: It lets each source word look at the other source words
It gives each target position a signal for its place in the output
It lets each target position look up the useful source words
It lets each target position look at the earlier target words
sorular.aciklama: In cross-attention the query comes from the decoder, and the keys and values come from the encoder, so the target side can get source information. Looking at earlier target words is the job of masked self-attention.

sorular.soru: When a GPT-style model answers a prompt, how do the answer tokens get information from the prompt?
secenekler: An encoder reads the prompt first, and cross-attention brings it to the answer
The causal mask hides the prompt, so the answer uses only its own tokens
The FFN stores the whole prompt, and each answer token reads it there
The prompt is earlier in the same sequence, so attention looks back at it
sorular.aciklama: A GPT-style model is only a decoder, so the prompt and the answer form one sequence, and each answer token can attend to all earlier tokens. Cross-attention needs a separate encoder, and this kind of model does not have one.

sorular.konu: Model families: BERT, GPT, T5 and MLM
sorular.soru: Most chatbots are built on decoder-only, GPT-style models. Why does this design fit a model that writes long answers?
secenekler: It reads the whole input in both directions before it starts writing
It learns to predict the next token, which is exactly how it writes
It looks up a separate encoder memory through cross-attention layers
It learns to fill in hidden words in the middle of a given text
sorular.aciklama: A decoder-only model is trained to predict each next token from the ones before it, and writing an answer repeats that task. Reading in both directions is what encoder-only models do, and it would show them the words they should predict.

sorular.konu: Model families: BERT, GPT, T5 and MLM
sorular.soru: BERT hides some input words and trains the model to guess them. What would happen if every word stayed visible during this training?
secenekler: The model could just copy each word, because it can already see it
The model could no longer see the words to the right of each word
The attention cost would grow, since no word is skipped in the scores
The model would lose the order of the words in the sentence
sorular.aciklama: An encoder sees the whole input in both directions, so a visible word would show the model its own answer. Hiding words does not limit the view to one side, because the model still sees context on the left and on the right.

sorular.soru: Many chat tools limit how long the input can be. Which feature of standard attention best explains why long inputs are expensive?
secenekler: Each token is read only after the one before it, so long texts take long
Each token adds one more attention head, so heads grow with the length
Each token gets a score with every other token, so work grows very fast
Each token needs its own embedding table, so memory grows with the length
sorular.aciklama: Standard attention scores every query against every key, so the number of scores grows much faster than the length. Reading tokens one after another is how an RNN works, and attention handles all positions in parallel.
